In the early-to-mid 1990s, the dominant hip-hop landscape was defined by regional warfare, street politics, and a focus on underground authenticity. Ghetto consciousness or street savvy was the primary marker in the rap scene for most of the 1990s. You wouldn't start seeing signs of a gradual shift until around 1995; this is where you get a blend of R&B, and the addition of Ghetto Fabulous starts to enter the picture, as well as rappers collaborating with mainstream pop acts. While the music was still grounded in the streets, several pivotal factors and artists laid the groundwork for the opulent, pop-friendly era to come.

In the mid-90s, artists began shifting their personas from street-level hustlers to high-earning crime bosses. This was exemplified by the fashion; it slowly went from oversized streetwear to mafia-style crime family fashion, as well as wearing all-black leather and shades.

The catalyst of the Jiggy Era was born directly out of the ashes of hip-hop’s darkest chapter. Between September 1996 and March 1997, the brutal murders of
brought a devastating climax to the East Coast–West Coast hip-hop rivalry. Before Biggie's untimely death, he released his last studio album,
which featured the track "Mo Money, Mo Problems" and its accompanying music video. With its shiny suits and fisheye camera angles, this song and video helped jump-start the Shiny Suit Era.
P-Diddy, or Puff Daddy at the time, was the undisputed architect of the era. His 1997 debut album
served as the movement's sonic manifesto. Puffy and his occasional counterpart, Mase, added a smooth, monotone foil to Puffy’s high-energy ad-libs. Ma$e’s effortless, laid-back luxury rap on

epitomised the "Shiny Suit" attitude. Will Smith, who returned to music with his 1997 smash hit "Gettin' Jiggy wit It", gave a catchier name for the era: the "Jiggy Era". Missy Eillot and Timbaland offered a different, avant-garde side of the same futuristic coin. Videos like "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)" utilised the same Hype Williams visual language but leaned into surrealism and afro-futurism.
The Jiggy Era was very short-lived, and signs of an eventual decline were already brewing; a lot of the motifs of this era were mostly caught up in Y2K New Year optimism, similarly to

, as the videos often leaned very heavily on disco and New Year's parties. The commercial homogenization alienated hip-hop purists. A fierce counter-cultural underground movement emerged in direct opposition to the "shiny suit" ethos. Too many solo acts and groups emerged after the East Coast-West Coast debacle; you had the Ruff Ryders, Dr Dre's successful return with 2001 (Album), Eminem, and Ludacris' debut and the growing emergence of Crunk or the southern invasion, with acts like Three Six Mafia, No Limit Soldiers, and Nelly. Its last gasp primarily continued with R&B, and by 2000 the trend already diminished, with the "bling era" fully taking over.
The visual style of the "shiny suit" or "jiggy" era (roughly 1997–1999) completely redefined hip-hop by trading street authenticity for high-budget, futuristic luxury. Driven heavily by stylists like

, the aesthetic was vibrant, expensive, and intentionally avant-garde. Settings would often include Las Vegas nightlife and Hollywood film production, as multiple music videos included action-film segments. But the most stand-out visual is the addition of shiny metallic suits. Whether it's power suits, tracksuits or jumpsuits, it would often be oversized and be the first thing you'd notice.

The visuals leaned heavily into maximalist wealth. Music videos frequently featured luxury speedboats, private helicopters, pristine foreign sports cars (like the yellow Ferrari F355), champagne rooms, and excessive diamond-encrusted jewellery.

In the jiggy era, the core message of mainstream hip-hop shifted from survival to institutional triumph. A casino floor is built entirely around the visual language of luck, risk, and massive payouts. This, along with Williams' signature fish-eye lens, gave way to a pristine look incorporated in jiggy era music videos. Casinos are windowless, clockless environments entirely disconnected from the real world, lit completely by neon and flashing slot machine displays. It also made for a cool backdrop style for dancers and raining money.

The disco revival of the Y2K era was used to describe how hip-hop producers—most famously Sean "Puffy" Combs and the Bad Boy "Hitmen" production team—hijacked the joyful, high-gloss DNA of late-1970s disco and early-1980s funk to create the soundtrack for the turn of the century. The aesthetic itself was meant to encapsulate disco incorporated into New Year's parties, especially for the countdown to the new millennium. Shiny Suits and disco balls would often be used in the videos along with samples from the 1970s and 1980s.

During the late 90s, hip hop and R&B often had crossover; this also affected hip-hop's signature sound of the early-mid 90s, widely known as boom-bap. Hip-hop was already known for sampling classic hit songs of yesteryear. The sampling obsession persisted, and hip-hop's more edgier street-wise grit was traded for more R&B-sounding songs with accompanying background vocals. This crossover created a fascinating paradox where rappers could still spit incredibly descriptive, street-wise lyrics, but the musical environment surrounding those lyrics was completely sanitised by R&B.

" era was a departure from the gritty, sample-chopping basement aesthetic of early-mid 90s hip-hop. Producers took massive, multi-platinum pop, funk, and disco loops from the late '70s and early '80s. They left the original groove almost entirely intact, counting on the listener's immediate nostalgia. The 1997 hit song "Hypnotize" by The Notorious B.I.G. famously samples the 1979 instrumental track "Rise" by jazz trumpeter Herb Alpert; "Mo Money Mo Problems" by The Notorious B.I.G. samples the 1980 disco hit "I'm Coming Out" by Diana Ross. As we ascend further into the jiggy era, R&B also uses key motifs of the jiggy era by sampling disco and including rappers like Ma$e, Puffy, and Jermaine Dupri.
The music videos of this era were multi-million-dollar cultural events, premiering on MTV’s

single-handedly transformed the rap video from a localised street document into a multi-million-dollar, pop-art blockbuster. Hype would use high production, with movie-like visuals which would often include lots of slow-mo, explosions, and glossy visuals. Hype did not invent the ultra-wide fisheye lens, but he made it a permanent fixture of hip-hop’s visual vocabulary. In Missy Elliott’s
, the lens paired with her inflated patent-leather suit to create a completely unforgettable, gravity-defying image.

Recently, those within Generation Z and Millennials have pointed out how the videos within the jiggy era and broader Y2K resemble the inside of a cheese grater, so the internet quickly turned it into a meme. This internet meme highlights a very specific, recurrent structural motif in Hype's work: hyper-reflective, texturised futurism. Instead of filming in front of flat walls, Williams built sets out of interlocking metallic plates, grid panels, and micro-perforated silver sheets. This made it look like it was filmed inside a kitchen cheese grater; with the use of the fisheye lens it made it all the more true.

As previously explained, when DMX and the Ruff Ryders broke through with their hit single "Ruff Ryders' Anthem" in 1998, it signalled the beginning of the end for the "jiggy" style of hip-hop and its accompanying music videos. Even the core rappers who had actively participated in the shiny suit era—such as Jay-Z, Nas, and Busta Rhymes—pivoted quickly to adapt to the changing cultural climate. This transition gave rise to the "Bling Bling" era, which introduced a brand-new mainstream appeal dominated by oversized sports jerseys, spinning medallions, and prominent video vixens.
